findings.text: A globally visible helper reports whether a newly loaded module is compatible with the active second-variant branch protection mode. When protection is disabled or the module carries the expected hardening, it reports success. Otherwise it records a sticky taint marker for later status rendering and reports incompatibility.

A globally visible notifier observes transitions of the unprivileged packet-filter enable state. It stays silent when disabling the feature, and otherwise emits a diagnostic only under specific enhanced-branch protection modes, with one mode further gated on whether threading is currently active.

Early boot entry points initialize first-variant branch protection. One selection step forces the selector to disabled when the CPU is unaffected or when global vulnerability policy declines mitigation. A separate application step programs entry-path fencing capabilities when automatic mode remains and vulnerability is present, then logs the chosen state. A dedicated command-line handler forces the selector to disabled.

Three boot phases manage return-bleed protection. Selection validates any explicit request against build inclusion and CPU support and resolves automatic mode by vendor and branch-protection state. A later update phase reconciles the choice with indirect-target and speculative-return states and with the active second-variant mode. A final apply phase programs entry barriers, return hooks and threading policy, then reports the result.

Three boot phases manage indirect-target selection protection. Selection disables the feature when the CPU is unaffected or policy declines it and checks build prerequisites and debug-alignment conflicts. An update phase refines the choice against the active second-variant branch mode and return-bleed stuffing state. An apply phase enables thunk-related capabilities and installs the appropriate return hook.

Two boot phases manage transient-scheduler protection. Selection disables the feature when the CPU is unaffected, derives automatic mode from which attack vectors require coverage, downgrades the choice when required microcode support is missing, and logs the outcome. Application enables user-kernel and virtualized buffer-clearing capabilities according to the selected scope.

Boot-option handlers translate textual mitigation requests into internal selectors. Return-bleed accepts a comma-separated list with enable, disable, technique and threading tokens. Indirect-target, transient-scheduler and user-space second-variant handlers each accept a single token from a small vocabulary. All reject missing input and ignore unknown tokens with a diagnostic.

Automatic first-variant handling forms a small decision graph. Unaffected CPUs take no action. Affected CPUs with automatic mode evaluate address-size control availability and speculative address-filter efficacy. When either indicates bypass risk, the machine enables kernel-entry fencing and conditionally enables user-entry fencing depending on swap-path vulnerability and page-table isolation state.

Return-bleed selection moves from explicit request through validation to resolution. Unsupported build or CPU combinations fall back to automatic with a warning. Valid explicit choices persist except on one vendor where later branch-mode state can override them. Automatic mode branches by vendor family and by barrier and enhanced-branch availability, with later overrides from indirect-target stuffing and speculative-return barrier states.

Indirect-target handling moves from vulnerability and policy gating through compatibility checks to mode refinement. Missing hardening build support or conflicting debug alignment forces disabled. A stuffing request without call-depth build support falls back to aligned-thunk mode. Guest-only scope without native-only vulnerability upgrades to full thunk mode. Final state further depends on whether the active second-variant mode is disabled, retpoline-based or fence-based.

Transient-scheduler automatic mode combines two independent coverage questions. User-to-kernel and user-to-user vectors contribute one scope, guest-to-host and guest-to-guest vectors contribute another. Either alone selects its partial scope, both together select full scope, neither leaves the feature disabled. Missing buffer-clear hardware support then moves any enabled choice to a microcode-missing state.

Across all families, absence of the corresponding CPU vulnerability marker forces the selector to its disabled state and skips further work. This holds for first-variant, return-bleed, indirect-target and transient-scheduler paths in both selection and update phases.

Speculative address-filter protection is treated as effective only when the CPU advertises the filter feature and is not marked vulnerable to the meltdown-class fault. Either missing feature or present meltdown vulnerability causes the check to report ineffective.

Call-depth tracking is considered usable only when both call-depth and retpoline build options are included and the active second-variant mode is one of the two retpoline-based modes. All other build or mode combinations report it unusable.

Choosing barrier-on-entry for return-bleed enables entry and guest-exit barrier capabilities while explicitly clearing software untraining, generic thunk and return-buffer fill capabilities that other mitigations may have set. Untrained-thunk and barrier modes may also disable threading when threading lacks a specific cross-thread guard and either an explicit threading option or global threading-mitigation policy requests it.

Option parsers share common contracts. A missing string argument is rejected with an error status. Return-bleed splits its input on commas and processes each token independently. Unknown tokens never change selection; they produce an error diagnostic and processing continues. One indirect-target build without mitigation support ignores its option entirely.

Each mitigation family scopes its kernel log output with a distinct textual prefix identifying return-bleed, indirect-target selection, transient-scheduler attacks and second-variant branch protection respectively.

Two build configurations provide alternative trivial helpers. One configuration renders a suffix indicating a tainted module load and reports sequential retpoline as active only when retpoline is present without fence-based retpoline. The other configuration always renders an empty suffix and always reports sequential retpoline as inactive.
The indirect-target selector distinguishes five abstract states covering disabled, automatic, guest-exit-only, aligned-thunk and retpoline-with-stuffing operation.

The return-bleed selector distinguishes seven abstract states covering disabled, automatic, untrained-thunk, entry-barrier, legacy branch protection, enhanced branch protection and call-depth stuffing.

The speculative-return selector distinguishes ten abstract states covering disabled, automatic, two microcode-missing conditions, microcode-provided, threading-disabled, safe-return, barrier and two barrier-scope variants.
The transient-scheduler selector distinguishes six abstract states covering disabled, automatic, microcode-missing, user-kernel boundary, virtualized and full coverage.

Kernel-side second-variant commands enumerate about ten choices across disabled, automatic, forced and several retpoline and enhanced-branch variants. User-side commands enumerate about eight choices across disabled, automatic, forced and policy-gated modes including privilege and sandbox scoped variants.

Global mitigation selectors are read-only after initialization. The active second-variant mode starts disabled, per-thread user selectors start disabled, and the indirect-target, return-bleed, transient-scheduler and command selectors start automatic when their build option is included and disabled otherwise. A threading-control flag starts false.

Each family maintains a read-only table mapping its internal selector value to a short human status line that distinguishes vulnerable from mitigated and names the active technique for informational logging.

Several combinations emit warnings and force fallback. Return-bleed stuffing without retpoline support falls back to disabled, indirect-target handling without retpoline and thunk support or with conflicting debug alignment or fence-based branch mode forces disabled, and vendor-mismatched thunk or non-protective branch choices warn that leakage remains possible.

Enabling unprivileged packet-filter execution while enhanced-branch protection is active warns of possible data leakage through branch-history attacks, with one combined fence-plus-threading configuration carrying its own distinct warning. A separate defined warning covers performance loss when legacy branch protection is chosen on CPUs with enhanced support.
